data.name: MiG-29 Fulcrum
data.detailed_description:
The Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-29 Fulcrum is one of the world's most maneuverable and toughest fighter jets and has often been compared to its closest Western counterpart, the F-16. Innovations unique to the aircraft allow MiG pilots to perform remarkable moves like the Tailslide and Cobra maneuvers. Exported to nearly 20 air forces, the MiG-29 continues to be a formidable world presence in the struggle for air-superiority.
Features
  • Authentic MiG-29 flight model developed with the assistance of Yuri Prikhodko, Russian MiG-29 test pilot/cosmonaut
  • Fast and furious combat with high definition graphics [1024 x 768 resolution with Voodoo2™ — incredible with SLI]
  • Highly detailed interactive cockpit
  • 40 single player missions plus 12 multiplayer missions — 6 deathmatch and 6 A.W. (Air War) cooperative missions
  • MiG-29 Fulcrum mission design tool to create your own sorties
  • 8 different camera views for exceptional situational awareness
  • Stunningly realistic landscapes
  • FREE Large-scale Internet play via NovaWorld — go head-to-head with over 120 F-16 Multirole Fighters, MiG-29 Fulcrums and F-22 Raptors in one arena

reviews.review:
MiG-29 Fulcrum is a classic combat flight simulator that captures a very different era of PC aviation games, when convincing aircraft behavior, large mission selections, and direct aerial combat mattered more than cinematic presentation or photorealistic graphics. Originally released in 1998, it was developed by NovaLogic and is published on Steam by NovaLogic and THQ Nordic. Its technology is unmistakably old today, yet there is still an appealing sense of purpose behind its design, particularly for players interested in historical combat flight simulations.

The main attraction is the MiG-29 itself. Rather than treating the famous fighter as little more than a recognizable aircraft model, the simulation attempts to communicate its reputation for agility and aggressive maneuverability. The flight model was created with assistance from Russian MiG-29 test pilot and cosmonaut Yuri Prikhodko, which was an impressive commitment to authenticity for a late-1990s PC game. Signature maneuvers such as the Cobra and Tailslide help emphasize the unusual capabilities of the aircraft and make learning its handling characteristics one of the most enjoyable parts of the experience.

Despite its simulation foundations, the game is relatively approachable compared with extremely technical modern military flight simulators. It wants players to understand their aircraft, but it also wants them to get into the air and start fighting. Dogfights can become fast and chaotic, requiring awareness of enemy positioning while making good use of the MiG's maneuverability. The balance between simulation and action gives it an accessible quality that remains useful today. Players can enjoy the fantasy of controlling a sophisticated fighter without facing an overwhelming wall of procedures before experiencing meaningful combat.

The interactive cockpit contributes greatly to the atmosphere. Its presentation obviously cannot compete with modern fully modeled cockpits, but it provides enough instrumentation and visual information to create a convincing sense of occupying the pilot's seat. Eight different camera views are available, which can be useful both for situational awareness and for simply enjoying the spectacle of the aircraft maneuvering. The external cameras are particularly enjoyable when performing aggressive turns or watching an engagement develop around the player.

Content is another notable strength. There are 40 single-player missions, providing a substantial collection of scenarios in which to practice flying and fighting. Rather than relying on a modern progression system filled with unlocks and rewards, the satisfaction comes from improving as a pilot and successfully completing increasingly demanding situations. A mission design tool is also included, allowing custom sorties to be created. This adds considerable replay value for players willing to experiment beyond the supplied missions.

The game additionally contains 12 multiplayer missions, consisting of six deathmatch and six cooperative Air War scenarios. Its original online ambitions were impressive, with NovaWorld once intended to support extremely large battles involving MiG-29s alongside aircraft from related NovaLogic simulations. However, this is a legacy title from 1998, so its historical online features should not be considered equivalent to an actively supported modern multiplayer environment. The single-player content and mission creation features are much stronger reasons to revisit it today.

Presentation is where its age becomes impossible to ignore. The landscapes, aircraft models, effects, textures, and interface are products of hardware from the late 1990s. What was once promoted as high-definition 1024 x 768 graphics is extremely modest by current standards. Terrain can appear sparse and repetitive, while visual effects lack the spectacle associated with contemporary aerial combat games. Even so, the simplicity has a nostalgic charm and keeps the screen relatively readable during combat. Players comfortable with retro PC graphics may find that the dated visuals quickly become secondary to the flying itself.

Its extremely modest original hardware requirements also demonstrate just how old the underlying technology is. Modern computers possess vastly more processing power than the game was designed to use, but age can create compatibility concerns independent of performance. This should therefore be approached as a preserved PC classic rather than a remastered simulation rebuilt for current systems.

Steam Deck compatibility is officially listed as Unknown. There is no official Steam Deck Verified or Playable rating, so handheld users should not assume a seamless experience. Its old Windows-focused design, keyboard-oriented controls, and lack of modern handheld optimization may require custom controller mappings or additional configuration. Players specifically purchasing it for Steam Deck should therefore regard compatibility as unverified rather than guaranteed.

What remains appealing is its focused identity. Instead of surrounding the aircraft with elaborate progression mechanics, the game concentrates on flying, combat, missions, and experimentation. The authentic-inspired flight model, large collection of missions, multiple viewpoints, interactive cockpit, and mission editor make it more substantial than its primitive appearance initially suggests. There is genuine satisfaction in gradually understanding how the fighter behaves and learning to exploit its maneuverability during combat.

MiG-29 Fulcrum is ultimately most worthwhile as a piece of combat flight simulation history. Its graphics and technical foundations have aged considerably, and anyone accustomed exclusively to modern simulators may struggle with its presentation. For retro flight-simulation enthusiasts, however, its straightforward combat, substantial mission selection, distinctive aircraft handling, and old-school design retain considerable charm. It is less a replacement for today's sophisticated simulators than an interesting reminder of how ambitious military aviation games could be with the technology of the late 1990s.

Rating: 8/10
